steps.explanationAfterStep: Histidine removes the serine proton as the oxygen attacks. The negative oxygen of the tetrahedral intermediate is held by two N–H groups of the protein backbone, the oxyanion hole. Aspartate, hydrogen bonded to the other ring nitrogen, holds the histidine in place and stabilises its positive charge.

The histidine now acts as a general acid: it gives back the proton, to the nitrogen, as the C–N bond breaks. The amine half of the peptide leaves as a neutral molecule, and the acid half stays bonded to serine as an ester, the acyl-enzyme.
Also correct: protonate the nitrogen first, then let it leave. In the enzyme the proton transfer and the C–N cleavage happen almost together.
The neutral amine leaves and the C=O re-forms: the acyl-enzyme.

title: Serine protease: acylation
subtitle: The catalytic triad cuts a peptide bond: serine attacks, the amine leaves
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 42
Berg, Tymoczko, Gatto and Stryer, Biochemistry (W. H. Freeman), chapter 9: catalytic strategies (chymotrypsin)

reactants.caption: model active site: N-methylacetamide (the peptide bond) + methanol (serine) + imidazole (histidine) + acetate (aspartate)
hintTiers: An alcohol is a poor nucleophile and an amide a poor electrophile. The enzyme's histidine acts as a general base: it takes the O–H proton as the oxygen attacks.
The imidazole nitrogen without a hydrogen takes the drawn O–H hydrogen, that O–H pair becomes the new bond from oxygen to the amide carbon, and the C=O π pair goes onto oxygen. Three arrows.
Imidazole nitrogen lone pair → new bond to the drawn hydrogen of methanol; that O–H bond → new bond from the methanol oxygen to the carbonyl carbon; C=O π bond → a lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen.
reactants.learnerPrompt: The serine oxygen attacks the amide C=O. Which group takes its proton?

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Serine's OH (pKa about 16) is far too weak an acid for histidine (pKa about 7) to remove on its own. The proton moves only as the oxygen bonds to the carbonyl carbon: general base catalysis.
Imidazole can attack acyl groups in the flask, but in the enzyme histidine is held next to serine to act as a base. Serine is the nucleophile.
Aspartate does not touch the serine. It sits behind the histidine and holds it in place by hydrogen bonding. Histidine is the base.
The amide nitrogen is not electrophilic. The carbonyl carbon is the electrophile.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right attack, but the serine oxygen would be left with three bonds and a positive charge. Which group takes its proton at the same time?

acyl-enzyme.caption: the acyl-enzyme (modelled by methyl acetate) + methylamine (the released amine half of the peptide) + imidazole + acetate

protonated-intermediate.caption: the tetrahedral intermediate with its nitrogen protonated + imidazole
hintTiers: The protonated nitrogen leaves as a neutral amine.
The O⁻ lone pair re-forms C=O and the C–N bond breaks onto nitrogen. Two arrows.
O⁻ lone pair → C=O π bond; C–N bond → a lone pair on nitrogen.
protonated-intermediate.learnerPrompt: Now the neutral amine can leave.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The serine oxygen could leave, but the protonated amine is now much the better leaving group.

tetrahedral-intermediate.caption: the tetrahedral intermediate (its O⁻ sits in the oxyanion hole) + the imidazolium ion (protonated histidine)
hintTiers: An amide nitrogen anion is a terrible leaving group. The histidine that took the serine proton now gives a proton to the leaving nitrogen: general acid catalysis.
The O⁻ lone pair re-forms C=O, the bond from the carbonyl carbon to nitrogen becomes a new N–H bond to the imidazolium hydrogen, and that N–H pair stays on the imidazole nitrogen. Three arrows.
O⁻ lone pair → C=O π bond; C–N bond → new bond from that nitrogen to the drawn imidazolium hydrogen; imidazolium N–H bond → a lone pair on the imidazole nitrogen.
tetrahedral-intermediate.learnerPrompt: The C=O re-forms. Which group leaves, and where does it get a proton?

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: MeNH⁻ (the conjugate base of an amine, pKa about 35) is a terrible leaving group. The amine leaves as a neutral molecule: histidine protonates the nitrogen as it goes.
Losing the serine oxygen again just reverses the first step. The amine half of the peptide is the group that leaves.

mechanismSummary: Serine proteases such as chymotrypsin cut peptide bonds with a catalytic triad: serine, histidine and aspartate. Here methanol models serine, imidazole histidine, acetate aspartate and N-methylacetamide the peptide bond. Histidine takes the serine proton as the oxygen adds to the amide C=O (general base catalysis), and the oxyanion hole stabilises the tetrahedral intermediate. Then histidine gives the proton to the nitrogen as the C–N bond breaks (general acid catalysis): the amine half leaves, and the acid half stays on serine as an ester, the acyl-enzyme. An amide is very unreactive on its own; the enzyme makes every proton transfer happen at the right moment.
